**Michael James Radford** (born 24 February 1946) is an English film director and screenwriter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT-1) He began his career as a documentary director and television comedy writer before transitioning into features in the early 1980s.

His best-known credits include the 1984 [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)") of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")_ starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt") and [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton") (in his final role), the [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") adaptation _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice\_(2004\_film) "The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)")_, the [true crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_crime "True crime") drama _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, and the 1994 Italian-language comedy drama _[Il Postino: The Postman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Postino:\_The\_Postman "Il Postino: The Postman")_, for which he won the [BAFTA Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Awards "BAFTA Awards") for [Best Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction") and [Best Film Not in the English Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Film_Not_in_the_English_Language "BAFTA Award for Best Film Not in the English Language"), and earned [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations for [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") and [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Radford was born on 24 February 1946, in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidencies_and_provinces_of_British_India "Presidencies and provinces of British India"), to a British father and an Austrian [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") mother. He was educated at [Bedford School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_School "Bedford School") before attending [Worcester College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester_College,_Oxford "Worcester College, Oxford"). After teaching for a few years, he went to the [National Film and Television School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_and_Television_School "National Film and Television School"), becoming a student there in its inaugural year.

Between 1976 and 1982, Radford worked as a documentary film maker, mostly on projects for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), covering subjects such as Scottish islanders on the [Isle of Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Lewis "Isle of Lewis") in the [Outer Hebrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Hebrides "Outer Hebrides") who believe in the literal truth of the Bible: _The Last Stronghold of the Pure Gospel_; the soprano [Isobel Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isobel_Buchanan "Isobel Buchanan"): _La Belle Isobel_; the singer songwriter [Van Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison "Van Morrison"): _[Van Morrison in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van\_Morrison\_in\_Ireland "Van Morrison in Ireland")_; and the self-explanatory _The Making of [The Pirates of Penzance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pirates\_of\_Penzance "The Pirates of Penzance")_. On the last two of these, Radford worked with the [cinematographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer "Cinematographer")[Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins"), who would later shoot two of Radford's feature films; _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)")_ and _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_. Another notable early work was _[Another Time, Another Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another\_Time,\_Another\_Place\_(1983\_film) "Another Time, Another Place (1983 film)")_ (1983), a feature film set in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and centred on a love story between a local woman and an [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[POW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Radford came to international attention with _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)")_, his adaptation of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s novel _[1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")_, starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt") as Winston Smith, and in which [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton") gave his final film performance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) The film was made in the time and place ([London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), April–June 1984) at which the book was set.

Radford's next film, released in 1987, was _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, a period drama set in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") during the 1940s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) Radford again wrote the screenplay, an adaptation of the novel by [James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist) "James Fox (journalist)") also called _White Mischief_.

Michael Radford is most widely known as the writer and director of the 1994 film _[Il Postino: The Postman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Postino:\_The\_Postman "Il Postino: The Postman")_, which Radford adapted from the novel _[Ardiente Paciencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardiente\_paciencia "Ardiente paciencia")_ by [Antonio Skármeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Sk%C3%A1rmeta "Antonio Skármeta").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT-1) The massive international success of the film (for many years it was the largest grossing non-English language film ever made) led to international acclaim for Radford and the star of the film [Massimo Troisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massimo_Troisi "Massimo Troisi"). Tragically, Troisi died, aged 41, the day after the filming of _Il Postino_ was completed. The film won many international film awards including the 'Best Film Not in the English Language' [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") for Radford, who was also nominated for the [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") and [Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Writing_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Writing Adapted Screenplay")[Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

In 2000, Radford's film _[Dancing at the Blue Iguana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing\_at\_the\_Blue\_Iguana "Dancing at the Blue Iguana")_ was released.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) In a departure from his more usual development technique, namely adapting novels, this film was largely improvised, although Radford shared the screenwriting credit with [David Linter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Linter?action=edit&redlink=1 "David Linter (page does not exist)").

In 2004, Radford directed _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice\_(2004\_film) "The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)")_ (2004).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) He adapted the [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") play (see: [Shakespearean comedies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_comedies "Shakespearean comedies")), and the film stars [Al Pacino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino") as [Shylock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shylock "Shylock") and [Jeremy Irons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Irons "Jeremy Irons") as [Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_(Merchant_of_Venice) "Antonio (Merchant of Venice)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) In 2007, he reunited [Demi Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demi_Moore "Demi Moore") and [Michael Caine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine") (who had already been together in 1984 for _[Blame it on Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blame\_it\_on\_Rio "Blame it on Rio")_) in _[Flawless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flawless\_(2007\_film) "Flawless (2007 film)")_, a diamond heist story set in 1960.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) His most recent film is _[Elsa & Fred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa\_&\_Fred\_(2014\_film) "Elsa & Fred (2014 film)")_ (2014), a romantic comedy starring [Shirley MacLaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_MacLaine "Shirley MacLaine") and [Christopher Plummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Plummer "Christopher Plummer").

Radford directed his first play in 2000, a [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") production of _[The Seven Year Itch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Seven\_Year\_Itch "The Seven Year Itch")_. This was an adaptation of [Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder")'s 1955 film starring [Marilyn Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Monroe "Marilyn Monroe").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Radford has a son, Felix (born 1991), from his first marriage to Iseult Teran. He also has a daughter, Amaryllis (born 2005), and a son, Linus (born 2010), with his current wife, Emma Tweed.

In addition to English (his first language), he speaks fluent Spanish, French, Italian, and some Mandarin.

In September 2013, he took part in the Clipper Round the World Sailing Race, in which he raced one of 12 identical 70-foot racing yachts from London to Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-3)

**Michael James Radford** (born 24 February 1946) is an English film director and screenwriter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT-1) He began his career as a documentary director and television comedy writer before transitioning into features in the early 1980s.

His best-known credits include the 1984 [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)") of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")_ starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt") and [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton") (in his final role), the [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") adaptation _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice\_(2004\_film) "The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)")_, the [true crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_crime "True crime") drama _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, and the 1994 Italian-language comedy drama _[Il Postino: The Postman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Postino:\_The\_Postman "Il Postino: The Postman")_, for which he won the [BAFTA Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Awards "BAFTA Awards") for [Best Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction") and [Best Film Not in the English Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Film_Not_in_the_English_Language "BAFTA Award for Best Film Not in the English Language"), and earned [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations for [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") and [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Radford was born on 24 February 1946, in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidencies_and_provinces_of_British_India "Presidencies and provinces of British India"), to a British father and an Austrian [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") mother. He was educated at [Bedford School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_School "Bedford School") before attending [Worcester College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester_College,_Oxford "Worcester College, Oxford"). After teaching for a few years, he went to the [National Film and Television School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_and_Television_School "National Film and Television School"), becoming a student there in its inaugural year.

Between 1976 and 1982, Radford worked as a documentary film maker, mostly on projects for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), covering subjects such as Scottish islanders on the [Isle of Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Lewis "Isle of Lewis") in the [Outer Hebrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Hebrides "Outer Hebrides") who believe in the literal truth of the Bible: _The Last Stronghold of the Pure Gospel_; the soprano [Isobel Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isobel_Buchanan "Isobel Buchanan"): _La Belle Isobel_; the singer songwriter [Van Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison "Van Morrison"): _[Van Morrison in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van\_Morrison\_in\_Ireland "Van Morrison in Ireland")_; and the self-explanatory _The Making of [The Pirates of Penzance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pirates\_of\_Penzance "The Pirates of Penzance")_. On the last two of these, Radford worked with the [cinematographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer "Cinematographer")[Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins"), who would later shoot two of Radford's feature films; _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)")_ and _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_. Another notable early work was _[Another Time, Another Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another\_Time,\_Another\_Place\_(1983\_film) "Another Time, Another Place (1983 film)")_ (1983), a feature film set in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and centred on a love story between a local woman and an [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[POW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Radford came to international attention with _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)")_, his adaptation of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s novel _[1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")_, starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt") as Winston Smith, and in which [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton") gave his final film performance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) The film was made in the time and place ([London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), April–June 1984) at which the book was set.

Radford's next film, released in 1987, was _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, a period drama set in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") during the 1940s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) Radford again wrote the screenplay, an adaptation of the novel by [James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist) "James Fox (journalist)") also called _White Mischief_.

Michael Radford is most widely known as the writer and director of the 1994 film _[Il Postino: The Postman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Postino:\_The\_Postman "Il Postino: The Postman")_, which Radford adapted from the novel _[Ardiente Paciencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardiente\_paciencia "Ardiente paciencia")_ by [Antonio Skármeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Sk%C3%A1rmeta "Antonio Skármeta").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT-1) The massive international success of the film (for many years it was the largest grossing non-English language film ever made) led to international acclaim for Radford and the star of the film [Massimo Troisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massimo_Troisi "Massimo Troisi"). Tragically, Troisi died, aged 41, the day after the filming of _Il Postino_ was completed. The film won many international film awards including the 'Best Film Not in the English Language' [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") for Radford, who was also nominated for the [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") and [Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Writing_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Writing Adapted Screenplay")[Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

In 2000, Radford's film _[Dancing at the Blue Iguana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing\_at\_the\_Blue\_Iguana "Dancing at the Blue Iguana")_ was released.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) In a departure from his more usual development technique, namely adapting novels, this film was largely improvised, although Radford shared the screenwriting credit with [David Linter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Linter?action=edit&redlink=1 "David Linter (page does not exist)").

In 2004, Radford directed _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice\_(2004\_film) "The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)")_ (2004).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) He adapted the [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") play (see: [Shakespearean comedies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_comedies "Shakespearean comedies")), and the film stars [Al Pacino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino") as [Shylock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shylock "Shylock") and [Jeremy Irons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Irons "Jeremy Irons") as [Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_(Merchant_of_Venice) "Antonio (Merchant of Venice)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) In 2007, he reunited [Demi Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demi_Moore "Demi Moore") and [Michael Caine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine") (who had already been together in 1984 for _[Blame it on Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blame\_it\_on\_Rio "Blame it on Rio")_) in _[Flawless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flawless\_(2007\_film) "Flawless (2007 film)")_, a diamond heist story set in 1960.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) His most recent film is _[Elsa & Fred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa\_&\_Fred\_(2014\_film) "Elsa & Fred (2014 film)")_ (2014), a romantic comedy starring [Shirley MacLaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_MacLaine "Shirley MacLaine") and [Christopher Plummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Plummer "Christopher Plummer").

Radford directed his first play in 2000, a [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") production of _[The Seven Year Itch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Seven\_Year\_Itch "The Seven Year Itch")_. This was an adaptation of [Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder")'s 1955 film starring [Marilyn Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Monroe "Marilyn Monroe").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Radford has a son, Felix (born 1991), from his first marriage to Iseult Teran. He also has a daughter, Amaryllis (born 2005), and a son, Linus (born 2010), with his current wife, Emma Tweed.

In addition to English (his first language), he speaks fluent Spanish, French, Italian, and some Mandarin.

In September 2013, he took part in the Clipper Round the World Sailing Race, in which he raced one of 12 identical 70-foot racing yachts from London to Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-3)

_**Nineteen Eighty-Four**_ (stylized as _**1984**_) is a 1984 British [dystopian film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopian_film "Dystopian film") written and directed by Michael Radford, based on [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s [1949 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four"). Starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt"), [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton"), [Suzanna Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanna_Hamilton "Suzanna Hamilton") and [Cyril Cusack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Cusack "Cyril Cusack"), it follows the life of [Winston Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Smith_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Winston Smith (Nineteen Eighty-Four)") (Hurt), a low-ranking civil servant in a war-torn London in [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Oceania (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a [totalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarian "Totalitarian") superstate ruled by [Ingsoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingsoc "Ingsoc") and its leader [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-7) Smith struggles to maintain his sanity and his grip on reality as the regime's overwhelming power and influence persecute [individualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individualism "Individualism") and individual thinking on both a political and a personal level.

_Nineteen Eighty-Four_ was Burton's last screen appearance; it was released two months after his death and is dedicated to him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-tcmnotes-8) It was released in the United Kingdom on 10 October 1984 by [Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films"). It received positive reviews from critics, with many highlighted Deakins' cinematography and use of [bleach bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_bypass "Bleach bypass"). It was nominated for a [BAFTA Award for Best Art Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Art_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Art Direction"), and won two [Evening Standard British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards") for Best Film and Best Actor.

## Plot

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Plot")]

In a dystopian 1984, Winston Smith endures a squalid existence in the [totalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarian "Totalitarian") superstate of [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_geography_of_Nineteen_Eighty-Four#Oceania "Political geography of Nineteen Eighty-Four") under the constant surveillance of the [Thought Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_Police "Thought Police"). He resides in London, the capital city of the territory of [Airstrip One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airstrip_One "Airstrip One"), formerly Britain, and works in a small office cubicle at the [Ministry of Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Truth "Ministry of Truth"), rewriting history as dictated by [the Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingsoc "Ingsoc") and its supreme leader, [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), who never appears publicly but instead appears only on propaganda posters, advertising billboards and television monitors. Smith attends mandatory public rallies at Victory Square (formerly [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square")), where citizens are shown propaganda films of the current war situation as well as contradictory and false news stories about Oceania's war effort to unite the civilized world under Big Brother's rule. While his co-worker and neighbour Parsons seems content to follow the state's laws, Winston, haunted by painful childhood memories and restless carnal desires, keeps a secret diary of his private thoughts, thus creating evidence of his [thoughtcrime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoughtcrime "Thoughtcrime"). However, he tries to do it out of sight of the telescreens, to maintain his safety.

His life greatly changes when he is accosted by his fellow Outer Party worker [Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Julia (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a mysterious, bold-looking, sensual and free-spirited young woman who works as a print machine mechanic in the Ministry of Truth, and they begin an illicit affair. During their first meeting in the remote countryside, they exchange subversive ideas before having sex. Shortly after, Winston rents a room above a pawn shop in the less restrictive proletarian area where they continue their liaison. Julia procures [contraband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraband "Contraband") food and clothing on the black market, and for a brief few months they secretly meet and enjoy an idyllic life of relative freedom and contentment together.

Their affair comes to an end one evening, when the Thought Police suddenly raid the flat and arrest them both. It is later revealed that a [telescreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telescreen "Telescreen") hidden behind a picture on the wall in their room recorded their transgressions and that the elderly proprietor of the pawn shop, Mr. Charrington, is a covert agent of the Thought Police. Winston and Julia are taken away to the [Ministry of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Love "Ministry of Love") to be detained, questioned and "rehabilitated" separately. There [O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Brien_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "O'Brien (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a high-ranking member of the Inner Party whom Winston had believed to be a fellow thoughtcriminal and agent of the resistance movement led by the Party's archenemy, [Emmanuel Goldstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Goldstein "Emmanuel Goldstein"), systematically tortures him.

O'Brien instructs Winston about the state's true purpose and schools him in a kind of [catechism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechism "Catechism") on the principles of _[doublethink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doublethink "Doublethink")_–the practice of holding two contradictory thoughts in the mind simultaneously. For his final rehabilitation, Winston is brought to [Room 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Room_101 "Room 101"), where O'Brien tells him he will be subjected to the "worst thing in the world", designed specifically around Smith's personal phobias. When confronted with this unbearable horror–a cage filled with wild rats–Winston's psychological resistance finally and irretrievably breaks down; he hysterically repudiates his allegiance to Julia. Seemingly subjugated and purged of any rebellious thoughts, impulses or personal attachments, Winston is restored to physical health and released.

Winston returns to the Chestnut Tree Café, where he had seen the rehabilitated thoughtcriminals Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford (themselves once prominent but later disgraced members of the Inner Party) who have since been "vaporized" and rendered [unpersons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspeak#Newspeak_vocabulary "Newspeak"). While sitting at the chess table, Winston is approached by Julia, who was similarly "rehabilitated". They share a bottle of Victory Gin and impassively exchange a few words about how they have betrayed each other. In spite of everything they have gone through, they still reaffirm their bond and express desire to see each other again. After she leaves, Winston watches a broadcast of himself on the large telescreen humbly and remorsefully confessing his "crimes" against the state and imploring forgiveness from the populace.

Upon hearing a news report declaring the Oceanian army's utter rout of [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_geography_of_Nineteen_Eighty-Four#Eurasia_and_Eastasia "Political geography of Nineteen Eighty-Four")'s forces in North Africa, Winston, appearing to have been deprived of his freedom to think and feel for himself and reduced to a mere shell of a man, soon to be deprived of his physical existence, looks at the still image of Big Brother that appears on the telescreen but then quickly turns away from it and looks in the direction of Julia with tears in his eyes as the words "I love you" are heard whispered in his voice.

## Production

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section's source code: Production")]

In the winter of 1983 the director Michael Radford asked his producer to try to obtain the rights to Orwell's novel, with low expectations that they were available. It turned out that the rights were held by Marvin Rosenblum, a lawyer in Chicago who had been trying on his own to get such a film produced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) Rosenblum agreed to become an executive producer, and while the producer Simon Perry raised the production money from [Richard Branson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Branson "Richard Branson"), Radford wrote the script, inspired by his idea to make a "science fiction film made in 1948".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) The script was finished in three weeks.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)

For the role of [O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Brien_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "O'Brien (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), [Paul Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Scofield "Paul Scofield") was originally contracted to play the part, but had to withdraw after sustaining a broken leg while filming _[The Shooting Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shooting\_Party "The Shooting Party")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-10)[Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins"), [Sean Connery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") and [Rod Steiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Steiger "Rod Steiger") were all then considered.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) Richard Burton, who was living in [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti"), joined the production six weeks into its shooting schedule[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) and insisted on his costume of a [boiler suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiler_suit "Boiler suit") being hand-made for him in [Savile Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savile_Row "Savile Row").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-12)

Some sources claim that [principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began on 19 March 1984, ending later the same year in October 1984.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-tcmnotes-8) It was released that same month, however, and a title card at the end explicitly states that it "was photographed in and around London during the period April–June 1984, the exact time and setting imagined by Orwell."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-13) The budget was originally £2.5 million, but this rose during filming and additional funds were required.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-14) The opening scenes showing the [Two Minutes Hate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Minutes_Hate "Two Minutes Hate") were filmed in a grass-covered hangar at [RAF Hullavington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Hullavington "RAF Hullavington") near [Chippenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chippenham "Chippenham") in Wiltshire.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-15) Some scenes set in Victory Square were also filmed at [Alexandra Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Palace "Alexandra Palace") in London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-16)[Senate House (University of London)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_House_(University_of_London) "Senate House (University of London)") was used for exterior shots of the [Ministry of Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Truth "Ministry of Truth").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The disused [Battersea Power Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea_Power_Station "Battersea Power Station") in [Wandsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Wandsworth "London Borough of Wandsworth") served as the façade for the Victory Mansions, and the [Beckton Gas Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckton_Gas_Works "Beckton Gas Works") in the [Docklands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Docklands "London Docklands") of [Newham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Newham "London Borough of Newham") was used as the setting for the proletarian zones. The pawnshop exterior, a pub scene and a scene with a prostitute were filmed in [Cheshire Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_Street "Cheshire Street") in the [East End of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_End_of_London "East End of London"), an area Orwell had visited and commented on in his first book, _[Down and Out in Paris and London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_and\_Out\_in\_Paris\_and\_London "Down and Out in Paris and London")_. The canteen interiors were filmed in a [disused grain mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Mills "Millennium Mills") at [Silvertown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvertown "Silvertown"). In contrast, the idyllic, dreamlike "Golden Country", where Winston and Julia repair for their first tryst and which recurs in Winston's fantasies, was filmed in the southwest county of [Wiltshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiltshire "Wiltshire") at a natural circle of hills called "Roundway", near the town of [Devizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devizes "Devizes"). The scenes on the train were shot on the [Kent and East Sussex Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_and_East_Sussex_Railway "Kent and East Sussex Railway"). The film shared a number of locations with [Terry Gilliam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Gilliam "Terry Gilliam")'s _[Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil\_(1985\_film) "Brazil (1985 film)")_, which was filmed the same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)

Radford and the cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins") originally wanted to shoot the film in black and white, but the financial backers of the production, [Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films"), opposed this idea. Instead, Deakins used a film [processing technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_processing "Film processing") called [bleach bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_bypass "Bleach bypass") to give a distinctive washed-out look to the film's color values. This technique was invented by the Japanese cinematographer [Kazuo Miyagawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuo_Miyagawa "Kazuo Miyagawa") for [Kon Ichikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kon_Ichikawa "Kon Ichikawa")'s film _[Her Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her\_Brother "Her Brother")_ (1960), in imitation of a more complicated process developed by Technicolor and Deluxe for the [1956 version of _Moby Dick_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moby_Dick_(1956_film) "Moby Dick (1956 film)")_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film)#cite\_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film)#cite\_note-18)_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-19) The process was recreated for this production by Key. The film is a very rare example of the technique being applied to every release print, rather than the [interpositive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpositive "Interpositive"), that was struck from the [original camera negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_camera_negative "Original camera negative"), or the internegative (struck from the interpositive); as the silver is retained in the print and cannot be reclaimed by the lab, the cost is higher, but the retained silver gives a "depth" to the projected image.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Release and reception

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Release and reception")]

_Nineteen Eighty-Four_ made its theatrical debut on 10 October in London and on 14 December in New York City.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-auto-20) It was released in the United States for one week in December 1984 at the [Egyptian Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grauman's_Egyptian_Theatre "Grauman's Egyptian Theatre") in Los Angeles to qualify for the [1985 Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/57th_Academy_Awards "57th Academy Awards") and grossed a house record of US$62,121, despite stormy weather.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-hv-21)

[Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ said the film was "admirable, bleakly beautiful", although "not an easy film to watch".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-canby-3)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") awarded it 3.5/4 stars, writing that it "penetrates much more deeply into the novel's heart of darkness" than previous adaptations, and describing Hurt as "the perfect Winston Smith".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-22)

The [review aggregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") has given it a 76% approval rating, based on 33 reviews, with an average rating of 6.8/10. The site's critical consensus states:

> _1984_ doesn't fully emerge from the shadow of its source material, but still proves a solid, suitably discomfiting adaptation of a classic dystopian tale.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-23)

_Filmink_ called it "brilliant, incredible to look at, and emotionally devastating."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-al-24)

The review aggregation website [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") has given it a rating of 67 out of 100 based on 8 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-25)

## Score controversy

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section's source code: Score controversy")]

Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(February 2017)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

[Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films") (formerly part of the [Virgin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Group "Virgin Group")), who financed the film, commissioned the British rock/pop duo [Eurythmics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurythmics "Eurythmics") to produce the music for the soundtrack after initially approaching [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"), who demanded a fee that Virgin deemed to be too high.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-26) Radford objected to Virgin's insistence on using the more pop-oriented [electronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") Eurythmics music, as the traditional [orchestral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral "Orchestral")[score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_score "Film score") originally intended for the film had been composed entirely by [Dominic Muldowney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Muldowney "Dominic Muldowney") a few months earlier.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-al-24)

Against Radford's wishes, Virgin exercised their right of final cut and replaced Muldowney's musical [cues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_(theatrical) "Cue (theatrical)") with the new Eurythmics contributions. One Eurythmics song, "[Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(Eurythmics_song) "Julia (Eurythmics song)")", was also heard in its entirety during the film's closing credits. However, Muldowney's main theme music (particularly the state anthem, "Oceania, 'tis for thee") was still prominently used in the film.

In November 1984 Virgin Records released the Eurythmics soundtrack album, containing considerably altered versions of their music heard in the film, under the title _[1984 (For the Love of Big Brother)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984\_(For\_the\_Love\_of\_Big\_Brother) "1984 (For the Love of Big Brother)")_. The album reached number 23 on the UK Album Chart, and was later certified Gold by the [BPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Phonographic_Industry "British Phonographic Industry") for sales in excess of 100,000 copies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-BPI-27) A song from the album, "[Sexcrime (Nineteen Eighty-Four)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexcrime_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four)_(Eurythmics_song) "Sexcrime (Nineteen Eighty-Four) (Eurythmics song)")", was released as a single just prior to the album and became one of Eurythmics' biggest hits, peaking at number 4 and was awarded a Silver disc for sales in excess of 250,000 copies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-BPI-27) The music video for the single made use of clips from the film. The track "Julia" was also released as a single which peaked just outside the Top 40.

Radford disowned Virgin's edit of the film containing the predominantly Eurythmics score and, during his acceptance speech at the [_Evening Standard_ British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards"), expressed his displeasure at Virgin's "foisting" the Eurythmics music on his film.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-auto-20) Radford withdrew the film from consideration at the [BAFTA awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA") in protest of Virgin's decision to change the musical score. Eurythmics responded with a statement of their own claiming no knowledge of prior agreements between Virgin and Radford/Muldowney and that they had accepted the offer to compose music for the film in good faith.

In 1999 Muldowney's complete orchestral score (24 tracks in total) was released on a special limited edition CD album under the title _Nineteen Eighty-Four: The Music of Oceania_, to commemorate the film's 15th anniversary. The CD booklet featured previously unseen production photographs and artwork as well as liner notes by Radford.

As of today, [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") owns the film's rights worldwide since they own both the Atlantic Releasing Corporation and the Virgin Films catalogues, and on their DVD release in North America in 2003, the film's colour is restored to a normal level of saturation and the Eurythmics contributions to the score were removed entirely and replaced with Muldowney's musical cues as Radford had originally intended—although both Eurythmics and Muldowney are still jointly credited in the opening and closing titles. This DVD release was quickly discontinued and currently remains out of print. This version had previously been shown by [Channel 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_4 "Channel 4") in the UK in the late 1980s. However, while the MGM DVD release of the film in the UK in 2004 features the desaturated visuals, it has the mixed Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtrack on the English- and French-language audio tracks, but the purely Muldowney soundtrack on the German- and Spanish-language audio tracks.

In 2013 the film was re-released on DVD in North America by TGG Direct on a double feature with _[Megaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megaville "Megaville")_ (1990), under licence from MGM. This DVD release also features the original mix of Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtracks, as well as the theatrical desaturated colour palette. In 2015 the film was released on Blu-ray in North America by Twilight Time in a limited 3,000 copy run, again, licensed by MGM. This release features the Eurythmics/Muldowney Soundtrack on one audio channel and Muldowney's orchestral score on another, as well as keeping true to the original colour scheme.

The version of the film which has been released on [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") services is the 2015 HD edition. It is available only with the original Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtrack.

The 2019 [Criterion Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Collection "Criterion Collection") release of the film features the original colour scheme (with a transfer supervised by the cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins")) and includes both the Eurythmics soundtrack and the original score composed by Dominic Muldowney.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-28)

## Awards

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section's source code: Awards")]

It won the Best British Film of the Year award at the [Evening Standard British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards"). It also won The [Golden Tulip Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Tulip_Award "Golden Tulip Award") at the 1985 [Istanbul International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_International_Film_Festival "Istanbul International Film Festival").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Home media

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section's source code: Home media")]

[International Video Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Video_Entertainment "International Video Entertainment") paid US$2 million for North American [home video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_video "Home video") rights, the fifth-biggest deal ever at the time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-hv-21) Their initial VHS & Betamax releases came out in 1985, with a later release in 1989. [Avid Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avid_Home_Entertainment "Avid Home Entertainment") released it on VHS in 1990 and again in 1994. In between the Avid releases, [GoodTimes Home Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GoodTimes_Home_Video "GoodTimes Home Video") released a VHS in LP mode in 1992. After acquiring ITC Entertainment Group, [PolyGram Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Video "PolyGram Video") released their VHS in conjunction with [Sundance Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundance_Channel_(United_States) "Sundance Channel (United States)") in 1996.

In 2003 [MGM Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Home_Entertainment "MGM Home Entertainment") released it on DVD in North America and in the UK a year later; the American DVD only contains Muldowney's score while the UK DVD contains the mix of his and Eurythmics' soundtrack. TGG Direct re-released it on DVD in 2013 as a double feature with Megaville. It has been released on Blu-ray twice, first by [Twilight Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Time_(home_video_label) "Twilight Time (home video label)") in 2015 as a limited 3,000-copy run and by [The Criterion Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criterion_Collection "The Criterion Collection") in 2019. Both of these editions contain both the original theatrical Eurythmics score and the alternate Muldowney score.

In 2024 it was released on 4K [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") in Germany and Hungary.

_**Nineteen Eighty-Four**_ (stylized as _**1984**_) is a 1984 British [dystopian film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopian_film "Dystopian film") written and directed by Michael Radford, based on [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s [1949 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four"). Starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt"), [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton"), [Suzanna Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanna_Hamilton "Suzanna Hamilton") and [Cyril Cusack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Cusack "Cyril Cusack"), it follows the life of [Winston Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Smith_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Winston Smith (Nineteen Eighty-Four)") (Hurt), a low-ranking civil servant in a war-torn London in [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Oceania (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a [totalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarian "Totalitarian") superstate ruled by [Ingsoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingsoc "Ingsoc") and its leader [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-7) Smith struggles to maintain his sanity and his grip on reality as the regime's overwhelming power and influence persecute [individualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individualism "Individualism") and individual thinking on both a political and a personal level.

_Nineteen Eighty-Four_ was Burton's last screen appearance; it was released two months after his death and is dedicated to him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-tcmnotes-8) It was released in the United Kingdom on 10 October 1984 by [Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films"). It received positive reviews from critics, with many highlighted Deakins' cinematography and use of [bleach bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_bypass "Bleach bypass"). It was nominated for a [BAFTA Award for Best Art Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Art_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Art Direction"), and won two [Evening Standard British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards") for Best Film and Best Actor.

## Plot

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Plot")]

In a dystopian 1984, Winston Smith endures a squalid existence in the [totalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarian "Totalitarian") superstate of [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_geography_of_Nineteen_Eighty-Four#Oceania "Political geography of Nineteen Eighty-Four") under the constant surveillance of the [Thought Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_Police "Thought Police"). He resides in London, the capital city of the territory of [Airstrip One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airstrip_One "Airstrip One"), formerly Britain, and works in a small office cubicle at the [Ministry of Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Truth "Ministry of Truth"), rewriting history as dictated by [the Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingsoc "Ingsoc") and its supreme leader, [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), who never appears publicly but instead appears only on propaganda posters, advertising billboards and television monitors. Smith attends mandatory public rallies at Victory Square (formerly [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square")), where citizens are shown propaganda films of the current war situation as well as contradictory and false news stories about Oceania's war effort to unite the civilized world under Big Brother's rule. While his co-worker and neighbour Parsons seems content to follow the state's laws, Winston, haunted by painful childhood memories and restless carnal desires, keeps a secret diary of his private thoughts, thus creating evidence of his [thoughtcrime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoughtcrime "Thoughtcrime"). However, he tries to do it out of sight of the telescreens, to maintain his safety.

His life greatly changes when he is accosted by his fellow Outer Party worker [Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Julia (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a mysterious, bold-looking, sensual and free-spirited young woman who works as a print machine mechanic in the Ministry of Truth, and they begin an illicit affair. During their first meeting in the remote countryside, they exchange subversive ideas before having sex. Shortly after, Winston rents a room above a pawn shop in the less restrictive proletarian area where they continue their liaison. Julia procures [contraband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraband "Contraband") food and clothing on the black market, and for a brief few months they secretly meet and enjoy an idyllic life of relative freedom and contentment together.

Their affair comes to an end one evening, when the Thought Police suddenly raid the flat and arrest them both. It is later revealed that a [telescreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telescreen "Telescreen") hidden behind a picture on the wall in their room recorded their transgressions and that the elderly proprietor of the pawn shop, Mr. Charrington, is a covert agent of the Thought Police. Winston and Julia are taken away to the [Ministry of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Love "Ministry of Love") to be detained, questioned and "rehabilitated" separately. There [O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Brien_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "O'Brien (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a high-ranking member of the Inner Party whom Winston had believed to be a fellow thoughtcriminal and agent of the resistance movement led by the Party's archenemy, [Emmanuel Goldstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Goldstein "Emmanuel Goldstein"), systematically tortures him.

O'Brien instructs Winston about the state's true purpose and schools him in a kind of [catechism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechism "Catechism") on the principles of _[doublethink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doublethink "Doublethink")_–the practice of holding two contradictory thoughts in the mind simultaneously. For his final rehabilitation, Winston is brought to [Room 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Room_101 "Room 101"), where O'Brien tells him he will be subjected to the "worst thing in the world", designed specifically around Smith's personal phobias. When confronted with this unbearable horror–a cage filled with wild rats–Winston's psychological resistance finally and irretrievably breaks down; he hysterically repudiates his allegiance to Julia. Seemingly subjugated and purged of any rebellious thoughts, impulses or personal attachments, Winston is restored to physical health and released.

Winston returns to the Chestnut Tree Café, where he had seen the rehabilitated thoughtcriminals Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford (themselves once prominent but later disgraced members of the Inner Party) who have since been "vaporized" and rendered [unpersons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspeak#Newspeak_vocabulary "Newspeak"). While sitting at the chess table, Winston is approached by Julia, who was similarly "rehabilitated". They share a bottle of Victory Gin and impassively exchange a few words about how they have betrayed each other. In spite of everything they have gone through, they still reaffirm their bond and express desire to see each other again. After she leaves, Winston watches a broadcast of himself on the large telescreen humbly and remorsefully confessing his "crimes" against the state and imploring forgiveness from the populace.

Upon hearing a news report declaring the Oceanian army's utter rout of [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_geography_of_Nineteen_Eighty-Four#Eurasia_and_Eastasia "Political geography of Nineteen Eighty-Four")'s forces in North Africa, Winston, appearing to have been deprived of his freedom to think and feel for himself and reduced to a mere shell of a man, soon to be deprived of his physical existence, looks at the still image of Big Brother that appears on the telescreen but then quickly turns away from it and looks in the direction of Julia with tears in his eyes as the words "I love you" are heard whispered in his voice.

## Production

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section's source code: Production")]

In the winter of 1983 the director Michael Radford asked his producer to try to obtain the rights to Orwell's novel, with low expectations that they were available. It turned out that the rights were held by Marvin Rosenblum, a lawyer in Chicago who had been trying on his own to get such a film produced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) Rosenblum agreed to become an executive producer, and while the producer Simon Perry raised the production money from [Richard Branson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Branson "Richard Branson"), Radford wrote the script, inspired by his idea to make a "science fiction film made in 1948".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) The script was finished in three weeks.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)

For the role of [O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Brien_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "O'Brien (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), [Paul Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Scofield "Paul Scofield") was originally contracted to play the part, but had to withdraw after sustaining a broken leg while filming _[The Shooting Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shooting\_Party "The Shooting Party")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-10)[Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins"), [Sean Connery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") and [Rod Steiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Steiger "Rod Steiger") were all then considered.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) Richard Burton, who was living in [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti"), joined the production six weeks into its shooting schedule[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) and insisted on his costume of a [boiler suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiler_suit "Boiler suit") being hand-made for him in [Savile Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savile_Row "Savile Row").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-12)

Some sources claim that [principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began on 19 March 1984, ending later the same year in October 1984.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-tcmnotes-8) It was released that same month, however, and a title card at the end explicitly states that it "was photographed in and around London during the period April–June 1984, the exact time and setting imagined by Orwell."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-13) The budget was originally £2.5 million, but this rose during filming and additional funds were required.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-14) The opening scenes showing the [Two Minutes Hate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Minutes_Hate "Two Minutes Hate") were filmed in a grass-covered hangar at [RAF Hullavington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Hullavington "RAF Hullavington") near [Chippenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chippenham "Chippenham") in Wiltshire.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-15) Some scenes set in Victory Square were also filmed at [Alexandra Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Palace "Alexandra Palace") in London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-16)[Senate House (University of London)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_House_(University_of_London) "Senate House (University of London)") was used for exterior shots of the [Ministry of Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Truth "Ministry of Truth").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The disused [Battersea Power Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea_Power_Station "Battersea Power Station") in [Wandsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Wandsworth "London Borough of Wandsworth") served as the façade for the Victory Mansions, and the [Beckton Gas Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckton_Gas_Works "Beckton Gas Works") in the [Docklands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Docklands "London Docklands") of [Newham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Newham "London Borough of Newham") was used as the setting for the proletarian zones. The pawnshop exterior, a pub scene and a scene with a prostitute were filmed in [Cheshire Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_Street "Cheshire Street") in the [East End of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_End_of_London "East End of London"), an area Orwell had visited and commented on in his first book, _[Down and Out in Paris and London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_and\_Out\_in\_Paris\_and\_London "Down and Out in Paris and London")_. The canteen interiors were filmed in a [disused grain mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Mills "Millennium Mills") at [Silvertown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvertown "Silvertown"). In contrast, the idyllic, dreamlike "Golden Country", where Winston and Julia repair for their first tryst and which recurs in Winston's fantasies, was filmed in the southwest county of [Wiltshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiltshire "Wiltshire") at a natural circle of hills called "Roundway", near the town of [Devizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devizes "Devizes"). The scenes on the train were shot on the [Kent and East Sussex Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_and_East_Sussex_Railway "Kent and East Sussex Railway"). The film shared a number of locations with [Terry Gilliam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Gilliam "Terry Gilliam")'s _[Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil\_(1985\_film) "Brazil (1985 film)")_, which was filmed the same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)

Radford and the cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins") originally wanted to shoot the film in black and white, but the financial backers of the production, [Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films"), opposed this idea. Instead, Deakins used a film [processing technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_processing "Film processing") called [bleach bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_bypass "Bleach bypass") to give a distinctive washed-out look to the film's color values. This technique was invented by the Japanese cinematographer [Kazuo Miyagawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuo_Miyagawa "Kazuo Miyagawa") for [Kon Ichikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kon_Ichikawa "Kon Ichikawa")'s film _[Her Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her\_Brother "Her Brother")_ (1960), in imitation of a more complicated process developed by Technicolor and Deluxe for the [1956 version of _Moby Dick_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moby_Dick_(1956_film) "Moby Dick (1956 film)")_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film)#cite\_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film)#cite\_note-18)_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-19) The process was recreated for this production by Key. The film is a very rare example of the technique being applied to every release print, rather than the [interpositive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpositive "Interpositive"), that was struck from the [original camera negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_camera_negative "Original camera negative"), or the internegative (struck from the interpositive); as the silver is retained in the print and cannot be reclaimed by the lab, the cost is higher, but the retained silver gives a "depth" to the projected image.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Release and reception

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Release and reception")]

_Nineteen Eighty-Four_ made its theatrical debut on 10 October in London and on 14 December in New York City.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-auto-20) It was released in the United States for one week in December 1984 at the [Egyptian Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grauman's_Egyptian_Theatre "Grauman's Egyptian Theatre") in Los Angeles to qualify for the [1985 Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/57th_Academy_Awards "57th Academy Awards") and grossed a house record of US$62,121, despite stormy weather.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-hv-21)

[Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ said the film was "admirable, bleakly beautiful", although "not an easy film to watch".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-canby-3)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") awarded it 3.5/4 stars, writing that it "penetrates much more deeply into the novel's heart of darkness" than previous adaptations, and describing Hurt as "the perfect Winston Smith".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-22)

The [review aggregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") has given it a 76% approval rating, based on 33 reviews, with an average rating of 6.8/10. The site's critical consensus states:

> _1984_ doesn't fully emerge from the shadow of its source material, but still proves a solid, suitably discomfiting adaptation of a classic dystopian tale.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-23)

_Filmink_ called it "brilliant, incredible to look at, and emotionally devastating."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-al-24)

The review aggregation website [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") has given it a rating of 67 out of 100 based on 8 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-25)

## Score controversy

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section's source code: Score controversy")]

[![Image 5: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film) "Special:EditPage/Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(February 2017)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

[Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films") (formerly part of the [Virgin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Group "Virgin Group")), who financed the film, commissioned the British rock/pop duo [Eurythmics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurythmics "Eurythmics") to produce the music for the soundtrack after initially approaching [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"), who demanded a fee that Virgin deemed to be too high.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-26) Radford objected to Virgin's insistence on using the more pop-oriented [electronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") Eurythmics music, as the traditional [orchestral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral "Orchestral")[score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_score "Film score") originally intended for the film had been composed entirely by [Dominic Muldowney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Muldowney "Dominic Muldowney") a few months earlier.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-al-24)

Against Radford's wishes, Virgin exercised their right of final cut and replaced Muldowney's musical [cues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_(theatrical) "Cue (theatrical)") with the new Eurythmics contributions. One Eurythmics song, "[Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(Eurythmics_song) "Julia (Eurythmics song)")", was also heard in its entirety during the film's closing credits. However, Muldowney's main theme music (particularly the state anthem, "Oceania, 'tis for thee") was still prominently used in the film.

In November 1984 Virgin Records released the Eurythmics soundtrack album, containing considerably altered versions of their music heard in the film, under the title _[1984 (For the Love of Big Brother)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984\_(For\_the\_Love\_of\_Big\_Brother) "1984 (For the Love of Big Brother)")_. The album reached number 23 on the UK Album Chart, and was later certified Gold by the [BPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Phonographic_Industry "British Phonographic Industry") for sales in excess of 100,000 copies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-BPI-27) A song from the album, "[Sexcrime (Nineteen Eighty-Four)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexcrime_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four)_(Eurythmics_song) "Sexcrime (Nineteen Eighty-Four) (Eurythmics song)")", was released as a single just prior to the album and became one of Eurythmics' biggest hits, peaking at number 4 and was awarded a Silver disc for sales in excess of 250,000 copies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-BPI-27) The music video for the single made use of clips from the film. The track "Julia" was also released as a single which peaked just outside the Top 40.

Radford disowned Virgin's edit of the film containing the predominantly Eurythmics score and, during his acceptance speech at the [_Evening Standard_ British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards"), expressed his displeasure at Virgin's "foisting" the Eurythmics music on his film.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-auto-20) Radford withdrew the film from consideration at the [BAFTA awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA") in protest of Virgin's decision to change the musical score. Eurythmics responded with a statement of their own claiming no knowledge of prior agreements between Virgin and Radford/Muldowney and that they had accepted the offer to compose music for the film in good faith.

In 1999 Muldowney's complete orchestral score (24 tracks in total) was released on a special limited edition CD album under the title _Nineteen Eighty-Four: The Music of Oceania_, to commemorate the film's 15th anniversary. The CD booklet featured previously unseen production photographs and artwork as well as liner notes by Radford.

As of today, [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") owns the film's rights worldwide since they own both the Atlantic Releasing Corporation and the Virgin Films catalogues, and on their DVD release in North America in 2003, the film's colour is restored to a normal level of saturation and the Eurythmics contributions to the score were removed entirely and replaced with Muldowney's musical cues as Radford had originally intended—although both Eurythmics and Muldowney are still jointly credited in the opening and closing titles. This DVD release was quickly discontinued and currently remains out of print. This version had previously been shown by [Channel 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_4 "Channel 4") in the UK in the late 1980s. However, while the MGM DVD release of the film in the UK in 2004 features the desaturated visuals, it has the mixed Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtrack on the English- and French-language audio tracks, but the purely Muldowney soundtrack on the German- and Spanish-language audio tracks.

In 2013 the film was re-released on DVD in North America by TGG Direct on a double feature with _[Megaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megaville "Megaville")_ (1990), under licence from MGM. This DVD release also features the original mix of Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtracks, as well as the theatrical desaturated colour palette. In 2015 the film was released on Blu-ray in North America by Twilight Time in a limited 3,000 copy run, again, licensed by MGM. This release features the Eurythmics/Muldowney Soundtrack on one audio channel and Muldowney's orchestral score on another, as well as keeping true to the original colour scheme.

The version of the film which has been released on [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") services is the 2015 HD edition. It is available only with the original Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtrack.

The 2019 [Criterion Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Collection "Criterion Collection") release of the film features the original colour scheme (with a transfer supervised by the cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins")) and includes both the Eurythmics soundtrack and the original score composed by Dominic Muldowney.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-28)
